A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across substantial revision and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on 75 LSC circuits across five Pythia models, including transfer, ablation, representational, and causal-intervention results.

after.justification: V2 retains original LSC results and adds SVA experiments, a learned two-route positive control, very-low-frequency evaluation, and few-shot accuracy studies.

M1.justification: The primary discovery procedure retains ACDC, KL-based pruning, factorized tree patching, and per-model threshold selection. The new tasks, control models, and attribution checks extend the experiments without replacing or modifying the proposed discovery pipeline.

E1.justification: V2 adds subject–verb agreement, a synthetic cue-controlled retrieval versus memorization task, evaluation of the previously excluded very_low LSC population, and few-shot copying scenarios. The reverse-copy and zero-distractor variants already existed in v1 and are retained.

E2.justification: The ACDC, EAP, EAP-IG, and random-edge comparisons are retained. Additional comparisons include LSC circuits evaluated against SVA circuits on their respective tasks (Appendix J) and a length- and token-matched scrambled-prefix comparator in the new few-shot study (Appendix L).

E3.justification: New protocols include SVA two-choice scoring and subject-number corruption, independent qualification of trained positive-control models, position-resolved attribution, and paired few-shot conditions. Appendix C.4 also revises the reported LSC discovery sample counts: v1 states 256 examples per circuit, whereas v2 specifies effective single-batch counts of 256, 256, 128, 96, and 64 across model sizes. This does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a successful pipeline positive control, independent edge-marginality analysis, position-resolved attribution checks, head-role threshold sensitivity and canonical-induction checks, and explicit mean-ablation analysis. SVA sensitivity checks examine mislabeled noun pairs and differences between ablation protocols. These address substantial questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: V2 adds draw-blocked permutation tests for SVA and positional analyses, paired McNemar tests and blocked permutations for few-shot effects, and variability across qualifying control models. The primary LSC three-draw design remains. Its transfer-test description changes from permutation testing to one-sided paired Wilcoxon testing, while the redrawn boost heatmap drops per-cell standard deviations.

E6.justification: New results include matched SVA transfer efficiencies of 0.940–0.992 (Table 14) and positive-control cross-route transfer efficiency of −0.056 ± 0.047 (Table 13). Retained analyses also change: universal-core convergence shifts move from 0.50–3.34 layers in v1 Table 59 to −0.40–0.00 in v2 Table 60. Some revised values conflict internally: v2 Tables 4 and 5 report different resample-ablation effect sizes.

T1.justification: Appendix E.6 introduces the normalized edge-marginality definition ρ = r/k and its interpretation relative to the matched-size selection boundary. The principal circuit and transfer equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central phantom-specialization claim and four main findings remain. The abstract and conclusion add a bounded SVA replication claim and restrict the ≥99% LSC recovery claim to models above 70M. V2 also explicitly excludes claims about specialization at token-position or within-component feature levels.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies interpretation: cross-draw variability no longer establishes that individual edges are causally irrelevant, zero-ablation collapse limits sensitivity, and SVA does not reproduce every LSC pattern. It adds limitations concerning position aggregation, residual token confounds, few-shot applicability, and the synthetic control's scope. The revised logit-lens findings also replace the slower, weaker-core interpretation with nearly matching computation and timing.

D1.justification: V2 supplies extensive SVA construction and filtering details, positive-control architecture and training hyperparameters, qualification thresholds, corruption procedures, and few-shot construction and timing information. It clarifies effective ACDC batch consumption, supplies the missing 1.4B batch size, documents mask nondeterminism, and explains head-role classification thresholds. The code/data access link is retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds Mueller (2024) and connects pruning ambiguity to overdetermination in counterfactual analysis. Fisher's 1966 reference is removed alongside the changed transfer-test description. The principal related-work coverage and positioning remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: Extensive paragraph and sentence rewriting spans the abstract, introduction, experimental explanations, interpretations, and appendices. V2 separates the canonical-copy mechanism discussion into its own subsection, reorganizes the positive-control material, and moves the statistical-testing summary from Appendix D to Appendix G. These changes exceed the insertion of new scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds the two-route task diagram and several experimental tables, consolidates duplicate displays, and moves key appendix comparisons into the main text. It redraws the transfer-boost heatmaps with a shared color scale, replaces full interchange matrices with an aggregated display, and revises logit-lens plots and captions.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly identifies the missing successful pipeline positive control as its most important limitation. V2 directly addresses this with six independently qualified models and adds a carefully bounded SVA replication, substantially strengthening validation beyond LSC. Positional checks, reproducibility corrections, and more cautious causal interpretations further improve credibility. The control remains limited to constructed models, and reporting inconsistencies persist, notably the conflicting effect sizes in Tables 4 and 5, but these do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.
